uniform-circular-motion.def: Motion in a circle at a constant speed. The velocity changes direction continuously, so the object accelerates toward the center.

centripetal-acceleration.def: The acceleration of an object moving in a circle, pointing toward the center, of size a_c = v²/r.

centripetal-force.def: The net force toward the center of a circular path, of size mv²/r. It is not a separate force: one or more real forces (tension, friction, normal force, gravity) supply it, and it is never drawn as its own arrow on a free-body diagram.

tangential-acceleration.def: The part of an object's acceleration along its velocity, which changes its speed. On a circle it adds to the centripetal part as a vector.

period-motion.def: The time for one complete trip around a circle (or one cycle of a repeating motion), T, in seconds. For uniform circular motion, v = 2πr/T.

frequency.def: The number of trips or cycles per second, f = 1/T, in hertz (Hz = 1/s).

banked-curve.def: A curve whose road is tilted toward the center. On a frictionless banked curve the horizontal part of the normal force supplies the centripetal net force, at one speed: tan θ = v²/(gr). Curves that need friction are treated in words only.

vertical-loop.def: A circle in a vertical plane, such as a loop-the-loop. At the top, gravity and the track's normal force both point to the center; the minimum speed there is when gravity alone supplies the net force, v = √(gr).

conical-pendulum.def: A mass on a string swinging in a horizontal circle so that the string traces a cone. The vertical part of the tension balances the weight, and the horizontal part supplies the centripetal net force.

circular-orbit.def: The circular path of a satellite or moon around a central body, with gravity supplying the centripetal net force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r), independent of the satellite's own mass.

kepler-third.def: For circular orbits around the same central body of mass M, T² = (4π²/GM)r³: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbit radius.
